title: Street Fighter cast say movie 'for the fans' - will they show up?
description: Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie versio
body: Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs."It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat."And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail. Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look."I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says."My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'". Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula."I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says."I think we could feel it when we first read the script."Critics, though, haven't been convinced.

schema.headline: Street Fighter cast say movie 'for the fans' - will they show up?

title: Flintshire: Nurse who stole £750,000 from vulnerable 99-year-old struck off
description: A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.Rebecca Lou
body: A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care. Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.Evidence presented showed more than £370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with £160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her £400,000 house. The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".She convinced the resident to pay £20,000 for a car and £9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.Burwood told the tribunal the woman asked her to withdraw cash from her bank account and make donations to charities each week.She claimed the donations, which were between £250 and £500 each time, would usually go towards charities that supported the blind or those with heart issues.Burwood said she would either put the cash in charity pots while she was out and about, or hand donations directly to staff in local charity shops.Her legal representative Victoria Rees said the resident had told her "she didn't want anything to be left by the time she died, as she didn't want the government to have her money", adding Burwood "didn't keep any records of the amount of money she withdrew or the amount of money she donated".The pensioner's bank referred the matter to North Wales Police and the force launched an investigation.The resident's bank account was frozen following concerns about spending, but Burwood attempted to have restrictions lifted and took the resident to a bank branch.Bank staff claimed Burwood was "almost blackmailing" the woman, and told her to ask for the accounts to be unlocked.The panel found Burwood told the woman she would not be able to take her on outings if she could not access her money.The hearing was told the resident later told safeguarding staff she was shocked by the amount of money that had been spent from her account.Another nurse also said they overheard Burwood tell the woman, "I will give you the money back" and "sign here".She reported the conversation as evidence of financial abuse and it was decided Burwood would only make supervised visits to the woman.Burwood claimed she had only been asking the pensioner to "sign a condolence card" and it was "not in relation to signing a document".She claimed the resident's eyesight was "very poor" so she had held the card for her, showed her where she should sign and stopped her from signing over the printed words in the card.Police investigated, but the woman did not want to take further action as she described Burwood as a friend, and believed she had "learned from her mistakes". The panel concluded there had been a significant imbalance of power in the relationship.In its ruling, the panel said Burwood had engaged in a "sustained, calculated course of conduct" and had manipulated the resident for personal gain.It added Burwood had taken advantage of the trust the woman had placed in her and "weaponised" it against her.The panel also found Burwood acted dishonestly by failing to tell her employer she held financial lasting power of attorney for a resident at the care home where she worked.It said her actions amounted to serious misconduct, breached fundamental nursing standards and caused both financial and emotional harm.In its decision, the committee said Burwood's actions were "deplorable" and she was "morally culpable", adding that public confidence in the profession would be undermined if a finding of impairment was not made.The panel determined Burwood's conduct was "morally reprehensible, showed premeditated behaviour and indicated a deep-seated attitudinal problem".It determined her behaviour fell far below the standards expected of a registered nurse.Burwood said she "deeply regretted her actions" adding she "saw the resident as her nanna" as an explanation for why she crossed professional boundaries.The victim has since died, but had only been left with enough money to pay for 23 months of care before the council would have had to step in.James Bradford, operations director at Bryn Yr Haul nursing home, said the team there was "deeply saddened by this incident" and "extend our sincere apologies to everyone affected"."The welfare and safeguarding of our residents remain our absolute priority," he said."We fully support the NMC's decision and, since these events, there have been changes in management, and our safeguarding policies and procedures have been reviewed to ensure the continued safety and wellbeing of everyone in our care."

title: Police feared Andrew might delay access by saying his home was King's
description: Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the
body: Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the King, according to legal documents.Senior officers were concerned the King's brother could argue it was not his property, and that separate legal permission would have to be sought before officers could enter it.Delaying access would have risked the loss of evidence, the force said.The background to Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February has emerged in legal documents, when police asked a judge for warrants to raid the former prince's homes.Lawyers for Mountbatten-Windsor successfully argued those warrants were unlawful in court last week.Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the US Department of Justice published material which showed his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.The BBC has approached Mountbatten-Windsor's representatives for comment and he has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.The arrest of the former prince, on 19 February, was on suspicion of misconduct in public office.On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, he said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment. "Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment."Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.The legal documents have emerged after a High Court hearing earlier this month in which Thames Valley Police accepted the warrants it used to search Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful.Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to successfully challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.But items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.Thames Valley Police force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.At the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland jailed over murder plot
description: A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.Johannes Na
body: A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard. During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday. The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes."You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country. "You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed."There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan."We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school. He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets."You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room. At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die."Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission."According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it. "I can kill someone and life will be wonderful."Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified".He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn't."Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he would have shot himself in the foot to get out of the "pickle" he was in.Flanagan said: "Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot Network, an organised criminal group sanctioned by the UK and the US due to its involvement in orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime."The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case."However, as recent events have shown, Counter Terrorism Policing will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK."Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.The Norwegian lawyers acting for the 19-year-old said they would work to have him transferred to Norway to serve his sentence. "Twenty years is a very severe sentence for a boy who was 18 when he was arrested," they said in a statement. "The other young people convicted in the related proceedings in Norway mainly received youth sentences or community sentences. "We will take the time to consider the sentence carefully, together with him, his family and his British legal team."Counter Terrorism Policing said it continued to investigate those suspected of helping Natland obtain firearms and a stolen car.In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and was later released under investigation.Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods, specifically a car.They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

schema.headline: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland jailed over murder plot

title: Tiger attack victim's medical records may have been breached
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on SaturdayByOliver Wright and Emily JohnsonY
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on SaturdayByOliver Wright and Emily JohnsonYorkshireUpdated 2 hours agoMedical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.Image source, Ella FordImage caption, An eyewitness took a photograph of the tiger at the wildlife park shortly before the incidentIn a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so."We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits."The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals. "We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses."Image source, Phil Bodmer/BBCImage caption, Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened to visitorsAn inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday heard that Chapman had died of "multiple traumatic injuries".Chapman had attended the park at about 13:30 BST on Saturday, climbed over two fences and entered the tiger enclosure.After the attack, park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended, who confirmed Chapman's death at the scene, the inquest was told.Senior coroner Nicola Mundy said Chapman had a history of mental illness, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had suffered previous bouts of psychosis. The inquest heard that the 24-year-old was under adult mental health services in Doncaster, but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements".The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and lived in Doncaster at the time of his death.Get in touchYour Voice

title: 'People call them pervert glasses but they give me independence'
description: 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech Image caption, Fraser Fleming says his glasses help him navigate public
body: 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech Image caption, Fraser Fleming says his glasses help him navigate public transport and read street signsByHayley Jarvis and Steven GoddenBBC ScotlandUpdated 16 October 2026 06:23 BSTFraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information."I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says. "If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace."Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years.They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public."People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online. Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people."We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says.  "We're using them to lead an independent life."Fraser, from Motherwell, told the BBC's Your Voice he would often take his glasses off if he thought there was a chance of a confrontation."I've got enough to worry about getting from A to B," he says."I'll just put the glasses away and have to rely on my other senses in order to navigate around, which is going to make life a lot more difficult for me."Image caption, Tracey Rogerson says the technology is a big part of her independenceTracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns."I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says.Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year.It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities. As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month.Image caption, Gordon Brown is severely sight-impairedThis means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year.He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked."Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip. "I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group. "You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses."Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees. The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices."The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments.Image source, Spill the TeaImage caption, Cosplay artist Spill The Tea says she was secretly filmed by someone wearing the glassesCosplay artist Spill The Tea was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed.She later discovered the footage was posted online.The performer, who has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated"."He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist.She says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities."For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says."They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them."In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life. "They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. "It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it." Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: 'People call them pervert glasses but they give me independence'

title: Aberfan disaster hero dinner lady honoured for saving five children
description: On 21 October 1966, as a primary school and surrounding homes in Aberfan were engulfed by slurry from a collapsed coal tip, a dinner lady was collecti
body: On 21 October 1966, as a primary school and surrounding homes in Aberfan were engulfed by slurry from a collapsed coal tip, a dinner lady was collecting money from pupils.Within moments, 144 people were dead, including 116 children, on what was the last day of class at Pantglas Junior School before the half-term holiday.But five children were saved that day by the heroic actions of Nansi Williams, who died shielding the group."Apparently she was holding as much of us as she could, and trying to get us under a table," said Aberfan survivor Paul Harries, who has spoken to the media for the first time. Harries, who was aged six at the time, was one of the five who was found alive under Williams' body. "She gave everything to give us a future, and she lost everything," he said. "Nansi Williams was a hero. A true hero. My hero."He continued: "If it hadn't been for Nansi Williams, then instead of 116 children dying that morning it would have been 121."It would have been us, 100%."As the 60th anniversary of the disaster approaches, Williams will be honoured with a purple plaque, external to commemorate her courage."She was trying to protect children," she said."She died, and they lived."Bickley believes there are many people who should be recognised for their courage on that day, but agreed Williams was a hero. "I think Nansi went way, way beyond what she needed to do," she said. "She could have saved her own life. She cared more for the children."Nansi's godson, Dai Powell, campaigned for greater recognition and said stories of what happened were passed down through his family for decades."My ultimate hero. No-one will ever touch her," he said."We'd all like to think we'd do the same thing, but until it happens we don't really know."Her heroism is just unbelievable."

schema.headline: Aberfan disaster hero dinner lady honoured for saving five children

title: Your child wasn't invited to the party - here's how to handle the disappointment
description: Your child didn't get a party invite - here’s what to doImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Being left off the party list is a sad time for littl
body: Your child didn't get a party invite - here’s what to doImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Being left off the party list is a sad time for little ones but there are ways to helpByJennifer MeierhansUpdated 7 hours agoIt's around this time of year when children start coming home with party invitations in their school bag. It's exciting and a sign they're making friends as they embark on school life. But what do you do when your child doesn't get an invitation?If your little one has been left off the list, here are some ways to help them cope. Understand it's a very common scenario Image source, Emma PharaohImage caption, Dr Sasha Hall says not being invited to a birthday party is going to happen to our children at some pointEducational and child psychologist Dr Sasha Hall, who's mum to a three-year-old boy and five-year-old girl, says the first thing to understand is that this scenario is "completely normal"."Unfortunately it's going to happen to all our children at some point in our parenting journey," she tells CBeebies Parenting Download.Dr Hall says while it may be tempting to get involved, it is not helpful in the long term."We can't remove all the obstacles, but we can give them the skills to manage," she says. "It's about building their resilience... what skills can we teach rather than change their outcomes?"Comedian, author and mum-of-two Cariad Lloyd says it is a "rough" position for a child to find themselves in. "When they're little, it feels like first love... everything feels so heightened, especially with the party thing. Everyone gets not invited to somebody's party."Plan an alternative activity as a distraction Image caption, Cariad Lloyd and Dr Sasha Hall joined CBeebies Parenting Download Dr Hall suggests planning an alternative activity for your child to focus on instead of the party."Yes, that child said you can't come, but let's find another friend you can do something else with," she says.Lloyd adds that the more the party situation crops up throughout their primary school years, the more you can explain the different outcomes to them."They will be invited to lots of parties and not invited to loads and you'll stop counting them," she says."They will come back and be like 'so-and-so was upset because they're not invited'. And you'll be like, 'oh, do you remember when you were not invited to that one's party?' They all kind of take it in turns so it becomes less dramatic."CBeebies Parenting DownloadHelping children navigate friendshipsExplain it's not about themDr Hall says it's important to explain to your child that the decision to leave them off the list is not about them."There are so many factors at play, especially with five to seven-year-olds, they're too little to have built up any kind of idea that they're naughty, it most likely has nothing to do with your child," she says.Lloyd agrees it's worth explaining possible reasons: "They can't afford to have 20 kids at a party so they're doing six instead and you didn't make the cut."Dr Hall says there could be a myriad of reasons why your child hasn't been invited."It's about the parents' own childhood experience - if they only had a couple of friends at that age they may be happy and comfortable with a smaller party - or they might want a big party in the hope of bringing their child out of their shyness."Acknowledge it will likely blow overDr Hall says parents should remember it is not until children are slightly older that friendships take on a deeper meaning, so what may seem like a big deal now is likely to blow over."Around the age of two is when we start seeing them show an interest in others, but it's still kind of parallel play," she says."And then it's around three to five where they're actually socially motivated to choose preferences. So they might say 'I played with this child today', but it's around about five to seven where those friendships become more stable and that they're really meaningful to the child."She says parents should give children plenty of time and opportunities to form friendships."There's a piece of research that looked at how do adults go from acquaintances to friends and it says it takes 40 to 60 hours - acquaintance to good friend is 200."We then can't assume that because you've gone to soft play and your child has seen that kid twice that therefore you can say that's your friend."For more advice on all aspects of parenting including friendship and shyness go to the CBeebies Parenting YouTube channel., external

schema.headline: Your child wasn't invited to the party - here's how to handle the disappointment

title: Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he is "only standing up for Ukraine's interests" after scathing criticism from Donald Trump, who said Kyiv's new
body: President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he is "only standing up for Ukraine's interests" after scathing criticism from Donald Trump, who said Kyiv's new wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries was a "disgrace".The US president, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import diesel, also said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".Zelensky, who has been angered by the diesel deal, said he could not accept it, because a gas agreement could come next. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" he said at an EU summit in Brussels.Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated over the diesel deal and curbs on Ukraine's battlefield satellite network.Zelensky's trip to Brussels, following a visit to London, has come at the end of a bruising week. As he arrived at the summit on Friday, where EU leaders rallied around him in support, Zelensky said it was good to be back among allies. "Leaders, real leaders," he said, in a possible sleight to the US president.At the summit, funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the agenda.The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.Zelensky said that while Ukraine could produce up to three times more drones, it "simply [doesn't] have enough money for that".A fundamental problem for Kyiv -  which cannot be easily fixed - is the chronic lack of US-made Patriot missiles to defend its towns and cities.Zelensky said he believed Europe did possess all the interceptors his country would need this winter but described them as being scooped up in a piecemeal fashion.Zelensky also addressed Ukraine's frayed relationship with the US, saying there are "many people with good hearts in America" who want "to be allies, not to divide or humiliate Europe".Trump has heavily criticised Zelensky for resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries earlier this week, because it could impact Moscow's ability to complete its part of the diesel deal, which will see 300,000 tonnes of diesel sent to "the American and global marketplace".As both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking each other's energy infrastructure, Trump suddenly announced a ceasefire on the facilities last week. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same, but Moscow said it had never agreed to the deal and continued its attacks. After three days, Kyiv resumed its strikes.Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine.The US president said he was "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he was "not a good guy for us to deal with"."He doesn't want to settle," Trump said. "He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't.""As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled."When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said of Zelensky: "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit."Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russia's oil facilities, because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US has made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices. Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump's standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections.At a news conference after the EU summit, Zelensky was asked if he felt that Trump was using him as a scapegoat for his own political problems. After a pause, the president broke into a grin, prompting laughter from the journalists in the room. "This is my answer," he said.The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and on Friday said it would "put more money straight into Putin's pocket to fund this war".His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.During the slowdown on Tuesday night, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning.On Friday, Zelensky called the slowdown a "very dangerous and unpleasant surprise", adding that Starlink speeds were still not fully restored.The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence-sharing - crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.Satellite images have revealed how Russia has almost finished building a drone base in just six weeks, and how Kyiv is continuing to fight back with its own air power.Experts have told BBC Verify that the new facility two miles (3.5km) from the Millerovo airbase, near the border in Russia's Rostov region, seems designed to accommodate powerful jet drones, linked to deadly strikes on civilian targets.The site was an empty field as recently as late August.Justin Crump, from risk intelligence company Sibylline, said the base signalled that Moscow intended to "increase the tempo of its strikes against Ukraine this winter".Meanwhile, imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor shows a Ukrainian missile attack has destroyed several Su-34 fighter bombers at the Borisoglebsk airbase in Voronezh region.A large burn mark, debris and significant damage are visible in the spot where an image taken days earlier showed several Su-34 fighter bombers lined up on the tarmac.Additional reporting by Thomas Spencer

schema.headline: Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'

title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feelin
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused".The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet.Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.The woman gave evidence on Friday from behind a screen at Southwark Crown Court in London, on the third day of Brand's trial.She told the jury the alleged incident at MTV lasted for about 20 seconds, adding: "It was a very short exchange."Asked how she felt after the alleged attack by Brand, the woman said: "Bewildered, confused, 'what the hell happened there?'"She said Brand went from someone who was "affable" to a "wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet"."I was confused that that actually just happened - anyone would be," she said.The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it."He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door."He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away."I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said. Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand."I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary."You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said."It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."The woman was speaking after a former flatmate of Brand's, Andrew Dobson, earlier told the jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer.Dobson gave evidence after another woman told the court on Thursday that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999.She said she had met Brand, before he was famous, while she was attending the Labour Party conference.Dobson told the court on Friday he attended the Bournemouth conference and had written music for a fringe event that Brand was part of.Karmy-Jones asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous.Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical"."I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term."Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand.He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand.The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members.The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard.Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried".The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?"Dobson replied: "I can't recall anything specific that was said. I only remember the atmosphere and panicked, urgent. Feeling tense and confusing."He went on to tell the jury there had been an "abrupt change of atmosphere" from what had been a "fun week" to an "abrupt change of tone".Under cross-examination by Brand's barrister, it was put to Dobson that in his witness statement he said that Brand was one of few men he knew that women would swoon over.Dobson replied: "He was certainly charismatic".Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual. The trial continues.

schema.headline: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault

title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moves from New Jersey prison to facility in Pennsylvania
description: Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.The
body: Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons. "His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on the tabloid reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports."For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.

schema.headline: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moves from New Jersey prison to facility in Pennsylvania

title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
description: The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development."Nature is
body: The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development."Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project."This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess."We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing."My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

schema.headline: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear L
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear Lyman, eastern UkraineA Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warningThe Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas regionHe is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front lineAn infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous"."The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unitIn Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation."As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed.""I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present."The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained."This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from dronesAll this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

title: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall
description: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.Joshua Foster t
body: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end."Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened."Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said. He described his client as an "incredible father"."[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."Do you have a story suggestion for Essex?
